newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's ousted Bhutto forced to move house.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's ousted Bhutto forced to move house.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, thronged by chanting supporters, moved out of her official residence into a private home on Tuesday, one week after being sacked on disputed charges of corruption.

"I think this whole thing stinks," Bhutto told an impromptu news conference at the home of Senator Gulzar Ahmed, where she will temporarily stay with her three children after vacating the prime minister's stately mansion.
Her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, who was investment minister in the ousted government, has been held without charge under a maintenance of public order law since Bhutto's dismissal.

About 200 activists from her Pakistan People's Party mobbed the black BMW sedan carrying Bhutto after it passed through the iron gates outside the prime minister's residence on its way to Ahmed's house in the capital Islamabad.

A crowd quickly surrounded the car, forcing it to stop. "Go Leghari, go!" the activists shouted, denouncing President Farooq Leghari, who dissolved the National Assembly and dismissed Bhutto's three-year-old government last week.
"Benazir step forward, we are with you!" the party workers chanted before the car sped off to Ahmed's house, a short distance away, where dozens of supporters forced their way in.
Bhutto, holding her three-year-old daughter Asifa on her lap, told reporters that her lawyers expected to file a legal petition on Wednesday morning asking the Supreme Court to reinstate her.
Bhutto said her dismissal and forced move were traumatic for her staff and children, who were going through the experience for the first time.
"But since this is the third time around with me, and because I had been hearing so many reports, that I was actually mentally geared up to the whole thing," she said.
A white wooden baby's crib stood nearby at the foot of the stairs, part of the few belongings Bhutto brought with her from the official residence.
"I look forward for early relief by the Supreme Court. I repudiate the charges the president has made," she said. "I expect the Supreme Court to do justice."
Bhutto lashed into Leghari, demanding that he step down as president. "I do not expect fair elections from Leghari," she said, referring to parliamentary polls set for February 3.

She was ousted in 1990 on similar charges. Her father, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, was Pakistan's first popularly elected prime minister, ruling from 1971 to 1977 when he was toppled by army chief General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq.
Zulfikar was hanged in April 1979 on a disputed conviction for conspiring to commit a political murder.
"I suppose that life has made me a bit tough," Benazir said.
"I haven't had an easy life, and for the last 20 years that I have been in politics, life has been very difficult. I've had my share of triumphs and I've had my share of tragedies."
